title: Russian Glide Bombs Kill at Least 30 at Kramatorsk Bus Stop
excerpt: A crowded bus stop in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region was struck around 10 a.m. Thursday; regional officials accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians as public transport was suspended in two cities.
body:
• Russian glide bombs struck a crowded bus stop and two city buses in Kramatorsk, in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, around 10 a.m. Thursday, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, local authorities said.
  • The death toll climbed through the day as rescue teams worked through the wreckage; local officials warned the count could rise further as the full extent of the damage is assessed.
  • Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, and authorities ordered public transport suspended in Kramatorsk and nearby Sloviansk amid fears of further strikes.
  • The strike came a day after a Russian missile destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, killing 22 people including five children, as Ukraine warned of an intensifying pre-winter wave of attacks.

At least 30 people were killed and 18 others wounded when Russian glide bombs hit a crowded bus stop and two city buses in Kramatorsk, the eastern Ukrainian city that has become a symbol of Kyiv's hold on the Donetsk region. The strike, one of the deadliest single attacks on civilians this year, landed on a street where the buses were running their morning routes at around 10 a.m. Thursday.

The local prosecutor's office posted photos of bodies and debris strewn across a road in front of the burning metal shell of a bus, according to Al Jazeera. Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb, and Kramatorsk's city council described the attack as "yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population."

A street with no military targets

Regional governor Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk military administration, said there was no question the strike was intentional. The city council echoed him: "Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets."

"For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible."

— Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk regional military administration

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the target as a bus stop and said rescue operations were underway. With the security situation deteriorating, Filashkin ordered public transport suspended in both Kramatorsk and the neighboring city of Sloviansk. "In such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers," he said.

There was no immediate comment from Moscow. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities and towns since its full-scale invasion began in February 2022.

Why Kramatorsk matters

Kramatorsk is one of the key cities Russia has not yet captured in Donetsk, a region Moscow claims as its own. It has served as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and sits in the so-called "fortress belt" — the string of fortified cities troops are fighting to keep hold of as Russian forces edge toward the city's eastern flank.

That strategic importance has made it a magnet for attack. Local officials say Russia has stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in recent months; in late August alone, as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in a single day. Glide bombs — converted Soviet-era munitions fitted with satellite-guided wing kits — have become a favored weapon for striking front-line cities from beyond the reach of Ukrainian air defenses.

The buses hit on Thursday were civilian transport on a civilian street. The attack follows a pattern of strikes on crowded public spaces that Kyiv has called deliberate terror.

A day earlier: Pryluky

The Kramatorsk strike came less than 24 hours after a Russian cruise missile directly hit a residential building in Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv. The death toll there rose to 22 on Thursday, including five children, and at least 54 people were injured, according to the regional governor. Rescue crews worked through rubble with search dogs while some survivors, with nowhere else to go, slept in damaged apartments.

The Associated Press reported that Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 142 drones overnight, of which defenses shot down or neutralized 126 — while strikes also hit Kyiv, where two people were found dead after a drone strike on a building and blackouts worsened across the capital.

What this means for the diaspora

The war's toll continues to land hardest on civilians, and its ripple effects still reach Indian households: energy prices, food costs, and the safety of the thousands of Indian students who once studied in Ukrainian cities. Thursday's strikes mark another step in the grinding attrition around the fortress belt that is shaping the war's next phase.

What's next

Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches, and appealed to NATO countries to turn statements of support into concrete defense packages — anti-ballistic systems, combat aircraft ammunition, and investment in interceptor drones. "It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote. Whether that aid arrives before the winter wave peaks will define the coming months of the war.
